title: Generative AI-assisted feedback and EFL writing: a study on proficiency, revision frequency and writing quality
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves EFL academic writing more effectively than traditional teacher feedback. The central question is how a commonly available AI writing assistant, Grammarly Premium, affects overall writing proficiency, revision behavior, and specific dimensions of writing quality in postgraduate EFL learners.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions in a pre-test/post-test control-group study. Sixty postgraduate students enrolled in an English for Academic Purposes writing course at a public university in Egypt were randomly assigned to an experimental group using Grammarly Premium and a control group receiving traditional written teacher feedback. The study ran for 6 weeks within an 8-week timeframe. All students completed the same writing tasks and were taught by the same instructor; the experimental group also received a training session on using Grammarly critically for revision.

Results showed that the AI-assisted feedback group outperformed the control group on the overall post-test writing score, with especially strong gains in Language Use and Organization. Content did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that the tool was more effective for surface-level and structural aspects of writing than for higher-order idea development. Within the experimental group, more frequent use of Grammarly’s generative and corrective features and more revisions were positively associated with better outcomes, and generative feature use during assignments predicted post-test performance beyond prior assignment scores. Qualitative interviews reinforced these findings by showing that students perceived the tool as increasing confidence, speeding revision, and improving accuracy, while also emphasizing the need for critical judgment and noting limitations in fluency and broader language support.

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered writing assistant and grammar/style feedback tool that provides automated corrective suggestions, clarity, style, vocabulary, and limited rewrite support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as Grammarly Premium to provide immediate AI-assisted feedback on EFL students’ drafts during practice and assignment writing tasks, compared against traditional written teacher feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized pre-test/post-test control group study with 60 postgraduate EFL students (n=30 Grammarly, n=30 control), the Grammarly group achieved significantly higher total post-test writing scores than the control group. The reported means were 54.37 (SD=5.54) versus 45.50 (SD=5.32), with Welch’s t(47.35)=10.89, p<0.001; Mann–Whitney U=16.50, z=6.42, p<0.001.

Effects varied by writing component. The Grammarly group did not differ significantly from control on Content scores (17.05 vs 16.10; t(58)=1.68, p=0.098), but it scored significantly higher on Organization (18.12 vs 15.65; Welch’s t(51.88)=4.31, p<0.001) and Language Use (19.20 vs 13.75; Welch’s t(40.15)=9.55, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Post-test writing component scores: Content, Organization, Language Use

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), higher feature use and more revisions were positively correlated with better post-test performance. Correlations with total post-test score were significant for generative AI use in practice (r=0.346, p=0.049) and assignments (r=0.373, p=0.032), grammar/vocabulary feature use in practice (r=0.374, p=0.032) and assignments (r=0.348, p=0.047), and total revisions in practice (r=0.359, p=0.040) and assignments (r=0.375, p=0.032).
findings.measure: Correlations between Grammarly usage behaviors/revisions and total post-test writing score

findings.finding_summary: In the Grammarly group (n=30), feature use was differentially associated with specific writing components. Generative AI feature use correlated significantly with Content (r=0.360 practice; r=0.369 assignment) and Organization (r=0.346 practice; r=0.389 assignment), and with Cohesion/Consistency for assignments (r=0.369). Grammar/vocabulary feature use correlated significantly only with Grammar and Vocabulary scores (r=0.415 practice; r=0.395 assignment).
findings.measure: Correlations between Grammarly usage behaviors and specific writing component scores

findings.finding_summary: More frequent use of Grammarly’s generative AI features was associated with more total revisions in the experimental group. The correlations were significant for practice activities (r=0.421, p=0.012) and assignment activities (r=0.398, p=0.018), suggesting that tool engagement was linked to a more active revision process.
findings.measure: Correlations between generative AI feature use and total revisions

findings.finding_summary: Hierarchical regression showed that assignment score explained initial variance in post-test performance (R2=0.162), and adding generative AI use during assignments improved the model by ΔR2=0.113 to a final R2=0.275. In the final model, assignment score (β=0.38) and generative AI use (β=0.34) were significant predictors; adding revision frequency did not significantly improve prediction (ΔR2=0.010).
findings.measure: Hierarchical regression predicting post-test writing score

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group study with random assignment after pretest, plus correlational and qualitative components. It is useful evidence, but it is not a full-blown RCT and includes subgroup-like descriptive analyses rather than true moderation tests.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on total writing score, organization, and language use are large and statistically robust, with substantial mean differences and strong t values. The study also reports meaningful positive associations between tool engagement and outcomes, indicating strong practical impact in this setting.
